Opening

BUILD · SCIENCE · W12B · 2 MINUTES

Choose Rock for the Job

Learning objective

I can compare candidates and justify a model-job choice with evidence and a limit.

Success looks like

  • Use the criteria in one stated brief.
  • Compare at least two candidates with relevant evidence.
  • Respond to a question by checking a gap or revising the choice.

The brief chooses the evidence columns. Compare two candidates, make a choice and check what is still unknown.

W12B · one 40-minute lesson

Seven stages, with one arrival and one exit. Use the route that helps you show your science today.

No earlier worksheet is needed. Fresh evidence is included.

Point, speak, sign, move cards, draw, write or direct an adult. Use one response mode; no separate participation form.

Arrival

BUILD · SCIENCE · W12B · 4 MINUTES

Four clues to start

Choose a route. Four checks help your teacher decide what support is useful today.

Supported · 4 questions

1. Read

Which candidate has 0.5 mL through-flow?

Help beside the question
Use the table.

Answer guidance

Answer: R.

2. Shape

Which has flat overlapping pieces?

Help beside the question
Read the final column.

Answer guidance

Answer: R.

3. Display

Which is patterned and polished?

Help beside the question
D or U?

Answer guidance

Answer: D.

4. Missing

U has no scratch result. Tested or not supplied?

Help beside the question
Keep the gap.

Answer guidance

Answer: Not supplied.

Standard · 4 questions

1. Compare

R gives 0.5 mL; D gives 3.5 mL. Which is lower?

Help beside the question
Same fixed method.

Answer guidance

Answer: R.

2. Purpose

Why might that matter for the rain-cover model?

Help beside the question
Water passage is a criterion.

Answer guidance

Answer: Lower through-flow is relevant to the stated barrier model.

3. Path

Name P’s two relevant supplied clues.

Help beside the question
Scratch and shape.

Answer guidance

Answer: Faint groove; even stable model piece.

4. Limit

Does a 120-second value prove permanent waterproofing?

Help beside the question
Time boundary.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

Stretch · 4 questions

1. Missing data

Why not treat U’s missing value as zero?

Help beside the question
Missing is not measured.

Answer guidance

Answer: No result was supplied; zero would invent evidence.

2. Compare

Why compare at least two candidates?

Help beside the question
Use the same criteria.

Answer guidance

Answer: To justify the choice relative to available alternatives.

3. Question

What question should challenge a path-safety claim?

Help beside the question
Think wet grip or loading.

Answer guidance

Answer: Where is the wet-grip, wear or load evidence?

4. Revision

Must a useful challenge always change the chosen candidate?

Help beside the question
It may change the claim or next check.

Answer guidance

Answer: No; evidence may keep the choice while narrowing the claim or adding a check.

Starter

BUILD · SCIENCE · W12B · 3 MINUTES

Choose for the path, not the roof

The brief is an even, surface-resistant path model. Which first choice uses relevant supplied evidence?

No answer chosen yet. Think or discuss first.

I do

BUILD · SCIENCE · W12B · 5 MINUTES

Make the science visible

Predict, model, explain

The brief needs __. I chose __ rather than __ because __. We still need __.

Choose each view. Describe the evidence before giving a conclusion.

R, P, D and U are fictional candidates. Keep the units, method and missing entries visible.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Water passage through a rock specimen is different from drainage through spaces between separate pieces. Surface wetting is not proof of through-flow. A scratch comparison is not a complete wear, slip, strength or construction test. These model briefs cannot approve real installations.

Local explainer · 32 seconds · silent with captions

Use instead of part of the demonstration. It never autoplays and needs no internet.

Full text / no-video alternative

00–08 seconds · Read the matrix
R, P, D and U are fictional candidates. Keep the units, method and missing entries visible.

08–16 seconds · Match the rain brief
R combines 0.5 mL through-flow with a supplied flat overlapping shape. This fits the simplified rain-cover brief.

16–24 seconds · Change the job
P offers the stronger supplied path-model clues. D matches a patterned indoor display. One candidate need not fit every job.

24–32 seconds · Add the missing check
U lacks test evidence. All real uses still need suitable checks; a classroom choice is not construction approval.

Use fictional job cards and supplied diagrams. No water or scratch practical is required. Do not build or approve a real roof, path or drainage installation.

Use the evidence together

Use a clue; explain the group

Select a card, then select its group. Keyboard, pointing and paper routes work too. You can move a card when your reasoning changes.

Rain-cover model

Path model

Indoor display

Needs another check

Select a card, then choose a group.

Would a small change help? · optional

You may ask for a clearer diagram, fewer cards at once, reading help or more thinking time. Tell your teacher, ask privately, point or pass. Your teacher will say what can change and check whether it helped. No extra sheet is needed.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Rain R over D; path model P using surface and shape clues; display D using finish and stability. Every claim remains limited to the simplified brief.

You do

BUILD · SCIENCE · W12B · 15 MINUTES

Show your science

Use today’s evidence

Fresh evidence desk

Choose the digital choices or matching paper. You do not need to complete both.

Fictional candidate matrix for classroom reasoning. Water values use 5 mL input, 120 seconds, matched prepared area/thickness and a checked seal. These are not class measurements or material certification.

CandidateWater below / mLScratch clueShape / appearance
R0.5Moderate markFlat overlapping pieces
P1.0Faint confirmed grooveEven stable path-model piece
D3.5Deeper groovePatterned polished indoor piece

Choose and read one brief.
Compare two matrix rows.
State evidence and one limit.
Check a question; revise or justify.

Supported · build your explanation

1. Choose

Pick rain cover or indoor display. Compare R and D.

Help: Read the relevant columns only.

2. Explain

Point to the value or feature supporting your choice.

Help: The brief needs __.

3. Check

Name or point to one missing check.

Help: Real installation is not approved.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Rain model R: lower water passage and flat overlap. Display D: patterned polished indoor piece. Accept fixing or long-term performance as a missing check.

Standard · build your explanation

1. Compare

Choose one brief and compare two candidates.

Help: Use units and shape/surface clues.

2. Justify

Give two relevant pieces of evidence.

Help: Do not add irrelevant scores.

3. Review

Check one teacher or peer question; keep or revise the choice.

Help: No compulsory written feedback record.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Rain R over D; path model P using surface and shape clues; display D using finish and stability. Every claim remains limited to the simplified brief.

Stretch · build your explanation

1. Evaluate

Compare three candidates and explain an exclusion.

Help: Missing evidence is not a zero value.

2. Challenge

Test a real-use claim against the supplied limits.

Help: Grip, wear, installation or time.

3. Refine

Narrow or revise the decision and state a further check.

Help: A unchanged choice still needs a reason.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

U cannot be assumed to perform well. Real-use claims need further property and installation evidence. Accept justified retained or revised choices.

Evidence-led choices

Use the digital choices or the matching paper page. One response mode is enough.

Revisit the model

R, P, D and U are fictional candidates. Keep the units, method and missing entries visible.

Refine one explanation

Check that the explanation follows the supplied observation and keeps the stated limit.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Rain R over D; path model P using surface and shape clues; display D using finish and stability. Every claim remains limited to the simplified brief.

Exit

BUILD · SCIENCE · W12B · 2 MINUTES

Two small checks

Supported · 2 questions

1. Rain

Choose R or D for the supplied low-through-flow, flat-piece brief.

Help beside the question
Read both criteria.

Answer guidance

Answer: R.

2. U

U lacks results. Guess or mark needs checking?

Help beside the question
Do not turn missing into zero.

Answer guidance

Answer: Needs checking.

Standard · 2 questions

1. Evidence

Give one reason P fits the path-model brief.

Help beside the question
Use a supplied clue.

Answer guidance

Answer: Faint groove or even stable model shape; include both for a fuller answer.

2. Limit

Does that prove wet-grip safety?

Help beside the question
Separate property.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

Stretch · 2 questions

1. Justify

Why is R preferable to D for this rain-cover model?

Help beside the question
Use data and shape.

Answer guidance

Answer: R has lower supplied through-flow, 0.5 versus 3.5 mL, and overlapping flat shape.

2. Question

How can a challenge improve a choice without changing the candidate?

Help beside the question
Narrow a claim or add a check.

Answer guidance

Answer: It can expose a missing property and add a required check while the model choice remains justified.

Learning objective

I can compare candidates and justify a model-job choice with evidence and a limit.

Key words

purpose — The job the material must do.

property — A feature we can observe or test.

permeability — How readily water can pass through a material.

criterion — A requirement used to compare choices.

Remember

  • Compare relevant columns, not every property equally.
  • Keep missing results visible.
  • Use units and the stated test conditions.
  • A model decision is not real installation approval.

Success looks like

  • Use the criteria in one stated brief.
  • Compare at least two candidates with relevant evidence.
  • Respond to a question by checking a gap or revising the choice.

The brief needs __. I chose __ rather than __ because __. We still need __.

TA Brief

Current stage

Current stage:

Preparation and access

Use fictional job cards and supplied diagrams. No water or scratch practical is required. Do not build or approve a real roof, path or drainage installation.

Scientific care

Water passage through a rock specimen is different from drainage through spaces between separate pieces. Surface wetting is not proof of through-flow. A scratch comparison is not a complete wear, slip, strength or construction test. These model briefs cannot approve real installations.

Responsive feedback within teaching

The lesson teacher hears an optional request, explains what can change, tries it and checks the effect. Passing or asking privately is valid. No compulsory participation task or new pupil form. Do not infer assessment codes from a click, download or written box.

Sources and scope

  • Original Made by Matt lesson
  • USGS: aquifers, porosity and permeability
  • BGS: building stone testing and selection

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Supported

Your task

1. Use these fictional teaching cards. All give sugar in g per 100 g: A — 4 g; B — 9 g; C — 14 g; D — 23 g.

Help with this question

Use a paper strip to track one card at a time. Say or point to the letter, the sugar number and ‘g per 100 g’ together.

2. Put the four cards in order from LEAST sugar per 100 g to MOST. Point, move paper cards or direct an adult.

Help with this question

Compare two numbers first. Place the smaller one towards LEAST, then find where each remaining card belongs.

3. Complete: Label ___ has the least sugar per 100 g. Label ___ has the most.

Help with this question

Look at the two ends of your own order. Use those card letters to fill the gaps.

4. Choose the claim we can support: 'A has less sugar per 100 g than D' / 'A is the healthiest food for everyone'.

Help with this question

Ask: does this sentence describe the sugar evidence, or claim to know everything about the food?

5. Finish or point: These sugar numbers show ONE PART OF NUTRITION / THE WHOLE EATING PATTERN. Keep “g per 100 g” with each number.

Help with this question

Look at what was measured. Think about whether these cards show every nutrient and everything a person eats.

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Standard

Your task

1. Read these fictional teaching labels. Each is PER 100 g. A: carbohydrate 22 g; of which sugars 4 g. B: carbohydrate 67 g; of which sugars 9 g. C: carbohydrate 58 g; of which sugars 14 g. D: carbohydrate 72 g; of which sugars 23 g.

Help with this question

Track the ‘of which sugars’ row. Keep the carbohydrate and sugar rows separate.

2. Make a results row for each label. Copy the SUGAR value with its unit and basis; do not copy total carbohydrate.

Help with this question

Use the headings Label | Sugar / g per 100 g. Check each copied value against its nutrient name.

3. Order A–D from least to most sugar per 100 g.

Help with this question

Check adjacent pairs: is each value no larger than the next? Recheck that all four use the same basis.

4. Write or say one comparison: 'Label ___ has ___ g sugar per 100 g. This is less/more than ___.'

Help with this question

Build the comparison from two complete readings. Include which label you are comparing it with.

5. Explain one thing these sugar numbers cannot tell us about the whole food or eating pattern.

Help with this question

Choose one missing piece of information. Explain why that missing information limits a wider judgement.

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Stretch

Your task

1. Fictional labels, all PER 100 g: A — carbohydrate 22 g, sugars 4 g; B — carbohydrate 67 g, sugars 9 g; C — carbohydrate 58 g, sugars 14 g; D — carbohydrate 72 g, sugars 23 g.

Help with this question

Identify the nutrient and reference amount before selecting numerical evidence.

2. Extract the four sugar values and order them. Keep the unit and basis.

Help with this question

Audit the completed order against the source labels; a correct number copied from the wrong row is still the wrong evidence.

3. Extra label E says 'sugars 3 g per 25 g serving'. Someone puts E before A because 3 is less than 4. Audit this decision.

Help with this question

Compare the reference quantities before comparing the two bare numbers.

4. Put E on a per-100 g basis before comparing. How many 25 g servings make 100 g? Then place E among A–D.

Help with this question

Find the scale factor from 25 g of food to 100 g of food. Apply the same factor to the sugar amount.

5. Write one supported comparison from A–D and repair this claim: 'The lowest-sugar card proves the best food for everybody.'

Help with this question

Separate a justified numerical comparison from a wider judgement. State exactly what the evidence establishes and what it leaves unknown.
